plain: Amendment 83 would write a right to hunt and fish into the Colorado Constitution. Hunting and fishing are already legal and regulated today.

short_version.text: Hunting and fishing are already legal, and Amendment 83 changes nothing right away. It would make them a constitutional right and the preferred way to manage wildlife, which could let courts strike down future limits. What "traditional methods" means is undefined.

agree_means: Agreeing adds a constitutional right to hunt, fish and take wildlife by traditional methods, and names hunting and fishing the preferred way to manage wildlife. The state could still regulate for science, safety or future hunting.
disagree_means: Disagreeing keeps hunting and fishing legal under current state and federal law. The legislature and the Parks and Wildlife Commission keep their current freedom to change the rules.

example.text: Colorado voters earlier approved limits on leghold traps and bear baiting. Opponents fear a hunter could challenge those limits as banning a "traditional method"; a supporter says Parks and Wildlife's rules would not change.

research_notes: Method: all pages were fetched directly (no browser needed) and every quote was checked against the fetched text. The BEA state sheet is a PDF at apps.bea.gov (value added is a national-accounts measure, not license revenue or total spending). Its table lists hunting, shooting and trapping at $215 million of value added in 2024 (27th among states) and boating and fishing at $736 million; I did not quote those rows because PDF table rows extract unreliably, so the text uses the sheet's headline figures only. The shared web-search budget ran out mid-task. Not found: Colorado Parks and Wildlife's own economic study of hunting and fishing, any polling on the measure, and any source tying the amendment to wolf policy. The amendment text covers species the state manages except nongame, endangered or federally protected-from-hunting species and does not mention wolves, so the wolf material is background on how contested wildlife rules already are, not an effect of the measure. Double-check: the 68 percent license-and-fee figure is the Common Sense Institute's, reported by the Colorado Sun (the Sun calls it a nonpartisan, conservative-leaning organization); I did not read the CSI report. The commission chair, Jay Tutchton, spoke for himself. The Sun's explainer is the source for the funding and committee details and for the leghold-trap and bear-baiting claims, which are opponents' reading. Dates marked accessed have no publication date.
